title: Daily Chatter: Trillion Dollar Babies - TheStreet
text:
The following article was first published at 10:09 a.m. eastern time as part of TheStreet's daily 'Chatter on The Street' global news snapshot. To learn or subscribe, please click here .
Trillion Dollar Babies Unprecedented. Awe-inspiring. Trump-enraging.
I could be talking about the historic pledge for peace by North Korea's leaders, and the incredible images of a handshake between Kim Jon Un and Moon Jae-In in the Demilitarized Zone that upstaged President Donald Trump's planned summit with Kim later next month.
But I'm not.
Amazon Inc. ( AMZN ) , the online retailing behemoth run by proverbial thorn-in-the-President's side, Jeff Bezos, is the talk of the markets this morning, with shares spiking to a record high (=6% to $1,322.86) after it obliterated Wall Street's first quarter earnings estimates, vaulting the Seattle, Washington-based group into second place - behind Apple - on the list of world's most valuable companies.
The numbers, in fact, have analysts talking - in serious terms - about the potential for two trillion-dollar companies (Apple is worth $830 billion, Amazon $760 billion) in the world's biggest economy, given the pace of earnings growth in the tech sector and consumers' willingness to spend cash in the digital realm.
Whether that comes to fruition or not, the tide of emphasis is clearly changing: in 2011, only two tech firms -- Apple ( AAPL ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ) -- cracked the top ten most valuable list. Today, tech comprises seven of the ten, with only Warren Buffet's Berkshire Hathaway, mega-bank JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ) and consumer goods giant Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ) getting a look-in. (Amazon, it's worth noting, is worth as much as JPM and J&J combined).
That shift has simultaneously powered U.S. markets and created a significant investor risk: nearly half of the S&P 500's first quarter gains are linked to three stocks (Amazon, Microsoft, Neltflix ( NFLX ) ) and 25% of the benchmark is now weighted to the tech sector, the highest portion since November 1999 - just months before the Nasdaq peaked on March 10, 2000 before collapsing 10% over the next week and extending that decline to around 75% by the October 2002 nadir.
Mind you, it's worth noting that the five FAANG stocks that have reported so far this quarter (Facebook, Amazon, Netflix and Google), have generated a collective $125 billion in sales. And, with Apple's release next week, that number is likely to jump past $200 billion, which means that total will easily top $1 trillion, even if growth rates slow, by the end of the year.
Away from tech, the dollar index, which benchmarks the greenback against a basket of six global currencies, traded near its 2018 high after a stronger-than-expected reading (+2.3%) for first quarter GDP in the United States. On the flip side, the pound fell sharply, to a six week low of 1.3765 against the dollar following data showing the U.K. economy grew at the slowest pace in five years (+0.1%).
Guess which economy has the most tech companies?
--Martin Baccardax, London Bureau Chief, TheStreet Inc.
